finalText:
`async` and `defer` both let the browser download a script while it keeps parsing the HTML. They differ in when the script runs, and neither does anything for an inline classic script. I couldn't open javascript.info (every URL I tried returned 404), so the answer rests on the WHATWG HTML Standard, MDN and web.dev.

**Parsing**
- Without either attribute, an external classic script is fetched and run immediately, and parsing stops until both are done. The spec says: "If neither attribute is present, then the script is fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)
- With `async`, the script is fetched in parallel and "evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)" (same spec page). When it runs, it can interrupt the parser. web.dev says async scripts "can interrupt DOM building if they finish downloading while the parser is still at work." (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript)
- With `defer`, the script is fetched in parallel and "evaluated when the page has finished parsing" (spec). It never interrupts the parser.
- Written together, `async` wins. MDN says: "If the attribute is specified with the async attribute, the element will act as if only the async attribute is specified." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script) The spec explains why authors do this: it makes legacy browsers that only know `defer` fall back to deferred behavior instead of blocking.

**Timing relative to DOMContentLoaded**
- `defer` scripts run after parsing finishes and before DOMContentLoaded. They also hold that event back. MDN's script page says: "Scripts with the defer attribute will prevent the DOMContentLoaded event from firing until the script has loaded and finished evaluating." The DOMContentLoaded page says the event fires once the document is parsed and "all deferred scripts (<script defer src="…"> and <script type="module">) have downloaded and executed." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event)
- `async` scripts are independent of DOMContentLoaded. The same MDN page says the event "doesn't wait for other things like images, subframes, and async scripts to finish loading."
- MDN's note on `readyState` goes further: DOMContentLoaded "is fired after the execution of these scripts, but before the execution of scripts with async." In practice an async script can run before DOMContentLoaded or after it. The spec only says it runs as soon as it's available, and web.dev only says it runs "before the window's load event." The sources therefore differ in emphasis. MDN's note describes the usual case, and the spec and web.dev make no promise either way. Don't depend on an async script running before or after DOMContentLoaded. If a script might run after the event, check `document.readyState` first, as MDN advises.
- The spec's processing steps back up the `defer` timing. Deferred scripts go into a "list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing," and async scripts go into a "set of scripts that will execute as soon as possible."

**Ordering with several scripts**
- `defer` keeps document order. MDN: "Scripts with the defer attribute will execute in the order in which they appear in the document." web.dev agrees that defer "ensures that scripts run in the order they appear in the HTML."
- `async` gives no order guarantee. web.dev: "it's possible (and likely) that async scripts won't run in the order in which they appear in the HTML." The spec treats async scripts as an unordered set, and each one runs when its fetch finishes.
- One related case is scripts inserted by JavaScript. Per the spec, a non-parser-inserted classic script with `src` and no `async` goes into an ordered "list of scripts that will execute in order as soon as possible."

**Inline classic scripts**
- `async` and `defer` have no effect without `src`. MDN warns for both attributes: "This attribute must not be used if the src attribute is absent (i.e., for inline scripts)… it would have no effect."
- The spec's algorithm agrees. The async and defer branches apply only if "el's type is "classic" and el has a src attribute, or el's type is "module"." Otherwise an inline classic script runs immediately, and it blocks the parser while it does.

**`type="module"` scripts**
- Modules are deferred by default. The spec says: "(The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts.)" MDN's script page says the same: "The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts — they defer by default." The MDN Modules guide adds: "There is no need to use the defer attribute (see <script> attributes) when loading a module script; modules are deferred automatically." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Modules)
- Deferred modules run in document order after parsing and before DOMContentLoaded. The spec appends them to the same after-parsing list as `defer` scripts, and MDN counts `<script type="module">` among the scripts DOMContentLoaded waits for.
- `async` overrides that. The spec says "the module script and all its dependencies will be fetched in parallel to parsing, and the module script will be evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)." MDN's wording is almost the same.
- Unlike classic scripts, modules don't need `src` for these attributes to matter. The spec's condition is "el's type is "classic" and el has a src attribute, or el's type is "module"". So an inline `<script type="module">` is deferred, and an inline module with `async` runs as soon as its imported dependencies are fetched. I'm inferring this from that condition. No page I opened states the inline-module case in so many words.

**Summary**
- Use `defer` for scripts that need the full DOM or depend on each other's order.
- Use `async` for independent scripts, such as analytics, where order doesn't matter.
- Plain `type="module"` already behaves like `defer`.
- Neither attribute does anything for inline classic scripts.
